title: SAT Solver Settles Erdős Discrepancy Problem for C = 2 (n = 1,161) via 13 GB Machine-Checked Proof
whyItMatters: Cracked the 82-year-old C = 2 case of the Erdős Discrepancy Problem with an exact bound (n = 1,161) and a 13 GB DRUP proof—the largest mathematical proof of its era and direct catalyst for Boolean Pythagorean Triples.
summary: Posted to arXiv on February 10, 2014 (published at SAT 2014), Boris Konev and Alexei Lisitsa at the University of Liverpool encoded the C = 2 case of Paul Erdős’s 1932 Discrepancy Problem into Boolean satisfiability. Using the Glucose and Plingeling SAT solvers, they proved that while a ±1 sequence of length 1,160 with homogeneous arithmetic-progression discrepancy at most 2 exists, no such sequence exists for length 1,161. The resulting 13-gigabyte DRUP proof certificate—larger than all of Wikipedia at the time—was independently verified by formal proof checkers, preceding Terence Tao’s 2015 general analytic proof and inaugurating the era of gigabyte-to-petabyte SAT mathematics.
technicalHighlights: Established the exact threshold n = 1,161 for discrepancy C = 2, settling an 82-year-old open case of Erdős’s Discrepancy Problem.
Produced a 13 GB machine-checkable DRUP proof certificate—the largest verified mathematical proof at publication.
Demonstrated CDCL SAT solvers as first-class mathematical discovery engines, directly inspiring Boolean Pythagorean Triples (2016) and Schur Number Five (2017).
caveats: Resolved the specific finite case C = 2 (n = 1,161); the general theorem for all C was proved analytically by Terence Tao in September 2015.

scoreRationale.foundational: Solved an 82-year-old Erdős open case with exact tight threshold n = 1,161 via automated SAT reasoning.
scoreRationale.ripple: Directly triggered the Cube-and-Conquer SAT math wave (Boolean Pythagorean Triples, Schur Number Five, Keller’s Conjecture).
scoreRationale.verification: 13 GB DRUP unsatisfiability certificate independently verified by formal checkers and published at SAT 2014.
scoreRationale.velocity: Solved in hours of CDCL solver runtime after resisting decades of human and Polymath5 attacks.
